citations.quote: The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following statement.

Let $X,Y,Z$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces over one scalar field, let $F:X\to Y$ and $G:Y\to Z$ be compact linear maps, and set $A:=G\circ F:X\to Z$. For spectral regularization families $R^G_\alpha:Z\to Y$ for $G^\dagger$ and $R^F_\gamma:Y\to X$ for $F^\dagger$, and a parameter rule $(\alpha,\gamma):(0,\infty)\times Z\to(0,\infty)^2$, define $T_\delta(z^\delta):=R^F_{\gamma(\delta,z^\delta)}(R^G_{\alpha(\delta,z^\delta)}z^\delta)$ for $z^\delta\in Z$. The order is fixed by the factorization: first regularize $G$, then $F$; no general identity $A^\dagger=F^\dagger G^\dagger$ is part of this definition.
the exact datum is $y=Kx^\dagger\in Y$. Given an exact datum $y\in Y$, solving this inverse problem means finding a parameter $x\in X$ such that $Kx=y$.
Thus $K^\dagger y$ is the unique minimum-norm solution of $Kx=r$, and the orthogonal-range component is mapped to zero.
A family of filters $g_\alpha$ with residual filters $r_\alpha(t)=1-tg_\alpha(t)$ has qualification at least $p>0$

derivations.claim: The common singular system makes A=GF have singular values a_j=lambda_j mu_j and right/left vectors x_j,z_j. The source expansion yields x^dagger=sum a_j^nu w_j x_j and z=sum a_j^(nu+1)w_j z_j. The minimum-norm convention gives A^dagger z=x^dagger, G^dagger z=Fx^dagger, and F^dagger G^dagger z=x^dagger. The intermediate truth y^dagger=Fx^dagger is a G power-source element with witness v_j=lambda_j^(nu+1)w_j and norm at most rho.

For e_G=R^G_alpha z-y^dagger, the residual representation is e_G=-|G|^nu p^G_alpha(G*G)v. Hence its source witness norm is at most S_G rho. The first discrepancy inequality and the noise bound give ||G e_G|| <= (tau_G+S_G)delta; interpolation yields an exact-data first-stage error of order rho^(1/(nu+1))delta^(nu/(nu+1)).

The exact composite bias e_A=x^dagger-R_F_gamma R_G_alpha z has source witness (I-R_F R_G A)w with norm at most (1+C_F C_G)rho. Its forward residual is decomposed into the data perturbation, first discrepancy residual, second discrepancy residual, and the bounded composite transfer on the perturbation, giving ||Ae_A|| <= (1+tau_G+tau_F+C_F C_G)delta. Interpolation gives the first term in the claimed bound.

The second residual operator q_gamma has exact-data multiplier -p_F_gamma(lambda_j^2)(1-p_G_alpha(mu_j^2)) and noise operator norm at most S_F C_G. The previous second-stage residual, qualification at nu+1, and geometric spacing lower-bound gamma_l; the first-grid case uses z nonzero. Thus ||R_F_gamma_l|| is O(rho^(1/(nu+1))delta^(-1/(nu+1)).

The previous first-stage grid point has residual above tau_G delta. Comparing it with exact data costs at most S_G delta, and qualification at nu+1 bounds the exact residual by D_G(nu+1)rho alpha_prev^((nu+1)/2). Geometric spacing lower-bounds alpha_k, so the noise amplification ||R_G_alpha(zdelta-z)|| is O(rho^(1/(nu+1))delta^(nu/(nu+1)); the first-grid case follows because alpha_1 is fixed. This gives the noisy first-stage error bound.

Split the final error into the exact composite bias and the outer regularizer applied to the two-stage noise effect. The exact-data and noisy first-stage errors are bounded by steps 2.1 and 3.1; the outer norm is bounded by step 2.3 and the exact composite bias by step 2.2. Multiplication gives the two displayed radius/noise terms; since nu>1, both delta exponents are positive.

derivations.claim: From G*G=diag(9,16) and F*F=diag(4,1), the Tikhonov maps are diag(3/(9+alpha),4/(16+alpha)) and diag(2/(4+gamma),1/(1+gamma)).
Multiplying the two diagonal maps in the prescribed order gives A=diag(6,4) and the stated composite estimator coefficients.

The estimator coefficients converge to 1/6 and 1/4. Since A is invertible, AA^-1=A^-1A=I, so A^-1 satisfies all four Penrose equations and is A^+ by uniqueness; the same argument for F and G yields A^+=F^+G^+.

derivations.claim: Direct multiplication gives $FG=\frac12\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$ and $GF=A=\frac12\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$, which are unequal. Each of $F,G,A$ is nonzero with a one-dimensional image, so both factors are rank deficient and noncommuting.

Put $B=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$. Multiplication gives $AB=G$ and $BA=F$. Since $F$ and $G$ are self-adjoint idempotents, $ABA=(AB)A=GA=G^2F=A$, $BAB=(BA)B=FB=B$, and both $AB$ and $BA$ are self-adjoint. Thus $B$ satisfies all four equations in [F2], so $A^+=B$ by [F3].

The same equations show $F^+=F$ and $G^+=G$, because each is a self-adjoint idempotent and hence satisfies the four Penrose equations; uniqueness in [F3] identifies them. Therefore $F^+G^+=FG=\frac12B\ne B=A^+$. This refutes the universal identity.

finite_checks.result: A^+=B while F^+G^+=FG=B/2, so the product identity fails.
